title: Act I, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: In thunder and lightning on a deserted place, three Witches agree to meet again 'when the hurlyburly's done, when the battle's lost and won,' upon the heath, to meet Macbeth. Called away by their familiars, they chant 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' and vanish into the fog and filthy air.

context.history: Jacobean audiences took witchcraft seriously: the 1604 Witchcraft Act made conjuring spirits a capital crime. Storms were believed to signal disorder in nature and the state.

significance: The short scene sets the play's key paradox ('Fair is foul, and foul is fair') and its atmosphere of inversion before any human appears; Macbeth will echo the line in his first speech.
discussionQuestions: Think of a time something that looked good turned out bad, or the reverse. What made it hard to tell?
Where does setting appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with fate and free will?
